Samuel, Diane. I listened to the Aurora call and I want to give you one tool before the next one, because you did something well and something you can do better. What you did well was hold the floor. What cost you ground was the second half, when Karl kept moving the discussion to the revenue figure and you kept following him there. You do not have to raise your voice to bring a conversation back. You move the focus with the sentence itself. Instead of saying the indemnification clause triggered this dispute, say it was the indemnification clause that triggered this dispute. Instead of saying they did not disclose the lien, say what they failed to disclose was the lien. The information is identical. What changes is where the listener has to look, and you did not have to speak faster or louder to do it.

Samuel, Karl again. Quick one, and it is about the back of the document. My team flagged three things in what you would probably call the boilerplate. First, the entire agreement clause is drafted so widely that it may exclude the side letter we signed in June, and that side letter is the only place the cure period is written down. Second, there is no severability provision at all, which for a contract governed by English law is unusual. Third, the notices clause still lists an address in Rio that my company left two years ago. None of this is commercial and none of it is why we are in this deal, but it is exactly the kind of thing that decides a case three years from now. Tell me what you want to do about each one.
